explanations.answer: Because He is the LORD their God
explanations.explanation: You got it, baker, and the reason is short. The verse says, “For I am the LORD your God.” (Leviticus 26:1) No long list and no fine print. Who He is is the reason on the page.

Stone does crumble, and I've watched plenty of cookies do it too. But crumbling isn't the reason the LORD gives. The verse says, “For I am the LORD your God.” (Leviticus 26:1) That's the whole answer.

explanations.answer: Because the nations will mock them
explanations.explanation: Mocking never comes up in this verse, friend. The nations aren't mentioned at all. The LORD says, “For I am the LORD your God.” (Leviticus 26:1) That's the reason, plain and simple.

True, baker. Right after the idols, the LORD says, “You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary. I am the LORD.” (Leviticus 26:2) Two more commands, back to back. He's building a list, and I'm taking notes with my mustache.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says, “You must keep My Sabbaths and have reverence for My sanctuary. I am the LORD.” (Leviticus 26:2) So the Sabbaths and the sanctuary both ride along with the no-idols command. Nothing in the verse takes them away.

That's the first thing on the list, baker. The LORD says, “I will give you rains in their season…” (Leviticus 26:4) Then the land yields its produce and the trees bear fruit. The rain comes first and the rest follows.

A king? Friend, that's a fun guess, but you went shopping in a different verse! The first thing the LORD names is “…rains in their season…” (Leviticus 26:4) After that come the land's produce and the trees' fruit. No throne in sight, just weather and fruit trees.

Gold! Baker, I like how you think. But gold has never watered a single field. The LORD starts with “…rains in their season…” (Leviticus 26:4) Then the land yields its produce and the trees bear their fruit.

True! The LORD says, “you will have your fill of food to eat and will dwell securely in your land.” (Leviticus 26:5) That means full plates and a safe place to enjoy them. Both blessings come in the same breath.

This one is true, baker. The LORD says, “you will have your fill of food to eat and will dwell securely in your land.” (Leviticus 26:5) So they eat their fill, and they live in the land securely. Nobody is going hungry in this promise.

The verse says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “I will rid the land of dangerous animals, and no sword will pass through your land.” (Leviticus 26:6) So the animals are cleared out, not left roaming. The peace goes all the way down.

False is right, baker. The LORD says, “I will rid the land of dangerous animals…” (Leviticus 26:6) He also says they'll lie down with nothing to fear. Fewer things lurking means better sleep for everybody.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “Five of you will pursue a hundred, and a hundred of you will pursue ten thousand…” (Leviticus 26:8) Five against a hundred is already wild. Then the numbers keep climbing.

Fifty is a big number, friend, but it's not the one in the verse. The LORD says, “Five of you will pursue a hundred…” (Leviticus 26:8) That's five Israelites chasing a hundred enemies. Then it jumps to ten thousand, and I need to sit down.
Twenty would already be a good day, baker. But the verse says, “Five of you will pursue a hundred…” (Leviticus 26:8) That's the number the LORD gives. And the very next part jumps to ten thousand.
Yes, baker. The verse says, “You will still be eating the old supply of grain…” (Leviticus 26:10) The old grain isn't even finished yet. That's the kind of problem I'd like to have.

That's the one. The LORD says they'll need to clear out the old grain “…to make room for the new.” (Leviticus 26:10) The new harvest shows up before the old one is gone. Plenty is crowding the storeroom.

Wet grain? Nobody in this verse is fussing about soggy grain, friend! The LORD says, “You will still be eating the old supply of grain when you need to clear it out to make room for the new.” (Leviticus 26:10) The trouble here is having so much grain that the old has to be cleared out for the new. I'd take that trouble any day.

Small? Baker, this verse is the opposite of small! The LORD says, “You will still be eating the old supply of grain when you need to clear it out to make room for the new.” (Leviticus 26:10) You're still chewing on last harvest and the next one is knocking. I've had batches where I wished for that kind of problem.

Nothing in this verse says the grain is foreign, friend. The LORD calls it the old supply and the new one. (Leviticus 26:10) It's their own harvest, and there's a lot of it. The only trouble is where to put it all.

True, and this might be the best blessing on the list. The LORD says, “And I will make My dwelling place among you, and My soul will not despise you.” (Leviticus 26:11) Full fields are great. Having Him close is greater.

This one is true, baker. The LORD says, “And I will make My dwelling place among you, and My soul will not despise you.” (Leviticus 26:11) It comes right after the harvest blessings. He promises more than good crops.

That's right, baker. The LORD says He is the one “…who brought you out of the land of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves to the Egyptians.” (Leviticus 26:13) He points back to what He already did for them. He adds that He broke the bars of their yoke.

Babylon isn't named anywhere in this passage, friend. The LORD says He brought them out of “…the land of Egypt so that you would no longer be slaves to the Egyptians.” (Leviticus 26:13) Egypt is the place He points back to.
Assyria doesn't show up in this passage, baker. The LORD says He brought them out of “…the land of Egypt…” (Leviticus 26:13) That's the rescue He reminds them of.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, “I broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness.” (Leviticus 26:13) The bars are broken, and then they can walk upright. He gave them more than freedom from the yoke.

Ruling the nations isn't what this verse says, friend. The LORD says He “…broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness.” (Leviticus 26:13) The bars come off so they can walk upright.
Rest isn't what the verse names, baker. The LORD says He “…broke the bars of your yoke and enabled you to walk in uprightness.” (Leviticus 26:13) The gift is walking uprightly, with the yoke gone.

That's right, baker. The LORD says, “You will sow your seed in vain, because your enemies will eat it.” (Leviticus 26:16) They do the planting, and someone else gets the harvest. That's a hard thing to watch.
Neighbors aren't who the verse names, friend. The LORD says, “…because your enemies will eat it.” (Leviticus 26:16) The seed gets sown in vain, and the enemies eat it.

Locusts are a good guess, baker, but this verse doesn't mention them. The LORD says, “You will sow your seed in vain, because your enemies will eat it.” (Leviticus 26:16) The ones eating the crop are enemies.

explanations.answer: Flee when no one pursues them
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…you will flee when no one pursues you.” (Leviticus 26:17) Earlier they were the ones chasing, and now they're running from nobody. The blessing flipped all the way over.

explanations.answer: Hide when no one sees them
explanations.explanation: Hiding isn't what the verse says, friend. The LORD says, “…you will flee when no one pursues you.” (Leviticus 26:17) They run, and nobody is even behind them.

explanations.answer: Fight when no one leads them
explanations.explanation: Fighting isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says they'll be defeated by their enemies, and that “…you will flee when no one pursues you.” (Leviticus 26:17) Running is the word, not fighting.
Right, baker. The LORD says, “I will break down your stubborn pride…” (Leviticus 26:19) Pride is the first thing He names here. Then He goes on to the sky and the land.
Weapons aren't named in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “I will break down your stubborn pride…” (Leviticus 26:19) What gets broken down is inside the people.

Trade doesn't come up in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will break down your stubborn pride and make your sky like iron and your land like bronze…” (Leviticus 26:19) Pride is the thing broken down first.
The verse is harder than that, friend. The LORD says, “…your land will not yield its produce, and the trees of the land will not bear their fruit.” (Leviticus 26:20) It isn't less produce. It's none.

False is right, baker. The LORD says, “…your land will not yield its produce, and the trees of the land will not bear their fruit.” (Leviticus 26:20) There's no smaller harvest in this verse. The fields give nothing.

That's it, baker. The LORD says, “I will send wild animals against you to rob you of your children, destroy your livestock, and reduce your numbers…” (Leviticus 26:22) The roads end up desolate too. This is a heavy verse.

Locusts aren't named here, friend. The LORD says, “I will send wild animals against you to rob you of your children, destroy your livestock, and reduce your numbers…” (Leviticus 26:22) It's wild animals this time.

Hail isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “I will send wild animals against you to rob you of your children…” (Leviticus 26:22) The animals also destroy their livestock and reduce their numbers.

It's the other way around, friend. The LORD says the wild animals will “…destroy your livestock…” (Leviticus 26:22) Livestock is on the list, along with their children and their numbers. It's a hard verse.

False is right, baker. The wild animals will rob the Israelites of their children, “…destroy your livestock, and reduce your numbers…” (Leviticus 26:22) Their livestock is on the list. It's a hard verse to sit with.

That's the one, baker. The LORD says, “…if in spite of these things you do not accept My discipline, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me…” (Leviticus 26:23) They keep walking in hostility instead of accepting it. And He's still speaking.

Blessings aren't what the verse names, friend. The LORD says, “…you do not accept My discipline, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me…” (Leviticus 26:23) The thing they won't accept is His discipline.
Messengers don't show up in this verse, baker. The LORD says they “…do not accept My discipline, but continue to walk in hostility toward Me…” (Leviticus 26:23) Discipline is the word.
Yes, baker. The LORD says, “Though you withdraw into your cities, I will send a plague among you…” (Leviticus 26:25) Walls won't keep it out. They end up delivered into the hand of the enemy.
Fire isn't named in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “Though you withdraw into your cities, I will send a plague among you…” (Leviticus 26:25) The cities don't keep the plague out.
A flood isn't in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “Though you withdraw into your cities, I will send a plague among you…” (Leviticus 26:25) Going inside the city walls doesn't stop it.

True, baker. The LORD says, “…you will eat but not be satisfied.” (Leviticus 26:26) Ten women bake the bread in a single oven, and it's doled out by weight. They do eat, and it still isn't enough. I think this one is heavy.
This one is true, friend. The LORD says the bread will be doled out by weight, “…so that you will eat but not be satisfied.” (Leviticus 26:26) They do eat. It just isn't enough.

explanations.answer: On the remains of their idols
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, “…heap your lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols…” (Leviticus 26:30) I think this one hurts to read. It sits right next to the high places and the incense altars.

City gates aren't named in this verse, friend. The LORD says He will “…heap your lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols…” (Leviticus 26:30) It's a heavy line, and the place it names is the idols' remains.

The fields aren't named here, baker. The LORD says, “…heap your lifeless bodies on the lifeless remains of your idols…” (Leviticus 26:30) It's a heavy verse, and the place is the remains of their idols.

The verse says the opposite, friend. The LORD says, “…I will refuse to smell the pleasing aroma of your sacrifices.” (Leviticus 26:31) That comes right after He says He'll reduce their cities to rubble and lay waste their sanctuaries.

False is right, baker. The LORD says, “I will reduce your cities to rubble and lay waste your sanctuaries, and I will refuse to smell the pleasing aroma of your sacrifices.” (Leviticus 26:31) So the answer is the refusal, not the aroma.

Yes, baker. The LORD says, “…the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate…” (Leviticus 26:34) The land gets its Sabbaths while the people are in the land of their enemies. Verse 35 says it will have the rest it did not receive during the Sabbaths when they lived in it.
Harvests aren't what the land enjoys here, friend. The LORD says, “…the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate…” (Leviticus 26:34) What it gets is rest.
Borders aren't in this verse, baker. The LORD says, “…the land shall enjoy its Sabbaths all the days it lies desolate…” (Leviticus 26:34) The land is resting while it lies desolate.

explanations.answer: The rest it missed while Israel lived there
explanations.explanation: That's right, baker. The LORD says, “…the land will have the rest it did not receive during the Sabbaths when you lived in it.” (Leviticus 26:35) The rest it missed is the rest it gets.

explanations.answer: The rest its new owners give it
explanations.explanation: New owners aren't mentioned in this verse, friend. The LORD says the land “…will have the rest it did not receive during the Sabbaths when you lived in it.” (Leviticus 26:35) It's the rest the land missed while Israel lived there.

explanations.answer: The rest it earned from great harvests
explanations.explanation: Great harvests aren't what the verse points to, baker. The LORD says the land will have “…the rest it did not receive during the Sabbaths when you lived in it.” (Leviticus 26:35) The land gets rest it missed, not rest it earned.

explanations.answer: The sound of a windblown leaf
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. The LORD says, “…even the sound of a windblown leaf will put them to flight.” (Leviticus 26:36) Not a trumpet and not an army, just a leaf. I think this one is heavy.

explanations.answer: The cry of a single bird
explanations.explanation: A bird isn't in this verse, friend. The LORD says, “…even the sound of a windblown leaf will put them to flight.” (Leviticus 26:36) It's the sound of a leaf that sends them running.

explanations.answer: The shadow of a passing cloud
explanations.explanation: A shadow isn't what the verse names, baker. The LORD says, “…even the sound of a windblown leaf will put them to flight.” (Leviticus 26:36) It's a sound, and a small one.

The verse says the opposite, friend. The LORD says the survivors “…will waste away in their iniquity and will decay in the sins of their fathers.” (Leviticus 26:39) They aren't growing strong. This is a heavy part of the sermon.

False is right, baker. The LORD says, “You will perish among the nations…” and the survivors “…will waste away in their iniquity and will decay in the sins of their fathers.” (Leviticus 26:38-39) It's a hard stretch of the sermon.

You got it, baker. The LORD says, “…I will remember My covenant with Jacob and My covenant with Isaac and My covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land.” (Leviticus 26:42) Three names, and He remembers each covenant. After a long hard stretch, this is the turn.

explanations.answer: Every one of their past sins
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the verse says, friend. The LORD says, “…I will remember My covenant with Jacob and My covenant with Isaac and My covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land.” (Leviticus 26:42) What He remembers is the covenant.

The idols aren't what He remembers, baker. The LORD says, “…I will remember My covenant with Jacob and My covenant with Isaac and My covenant with Abraham, and I will remember the land.” (Leviticus 26:42) He remembers the covenants and the land.

True, baker. The LORD says, “…they will pay the penalty for their iniquity, because they rejected My ordinances and abhorred My statutes.” (Leviticus 26:43) The text gives that as the reason. It's a sober line.

This one is true, friend. The LORD says, “…they will pay the penalty for their iniquity, because they rejected My ordinances and abhorred My statutes.” (Leviticus 26:43) Rejecting His ordinances is the reason the verse gives.

The verse says the opposite, baker, and it's good news. The LORD says, “…I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God.” (Leviticus 26:44) Even in the land of their enemies, He keeps His covenant.

False is right, friend. The LORD says, “…I will not reject or despise them so as to destroy them and break My covenant with them; for I am the LORD their God.” (Leviticus 26:44) His covenant stays standing, even there.

Yes, baker. The verse says these are the laws the LORD established “…between Himself and the Israelites through Moses on Mount Sinai.” (Leviticus 26:46) Moses is the one the LORD sent to bring His people out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). That's the closing line of the whole sermon.

Zion is a fine mountain, friend, and I'd bake a cookie on it any day. But the closing verse says the LORD established these laws “…through Moses on Mount Sinai.” (Leviticus 26:46) Moses is the one the LORD sent to bring His people out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10). Nice swing, though. You picked a mountain with real heart!

Carmel! Baker, you picked a mountain, so you're in the right neighborhood. But the verse ends with the laws the LORD established “…through Moses on Mount Sinai.” (Leviticus 26:46) Carmel never comes up in this passage. The sermon wraps up right at Sinai.
